https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-08-30-o.text: The officials said the shortage leaves NATO vulnerable to potential Russian ballistic missile attacks, with limited capability to defend against even a single strike. The U.S. military has moved missiles to the Middle East to counter Iranian attacks, depleting European inventories. [1]Â The reported shortage follows a period of heavy U.S. interceptor use. A report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), compiled by Mark F. Cancian and Chris H. Park, stated that during the 39-day war with Iran, the U.S. used so many key offensive and defensive weapons that it will take three or more years to rebuild some of these stocks to pre-war levels. [2] The war, which began in early 2026, has also coincided with ongoing transfers of U.S. air defense assets to Ukraine, further straining available stocks. [3] Specifics of the Shortage and Defensive Gaps The U.S. defense official said NATO lacks enough Patriots to stop a sustained ballistic missile assault and would have "very limited" ability to intercept a single missile or stray projectile. The official compared a potential scenario to Ukraine's experience, saying NATO could be forced "to take punch after punch in the mouth." [1] Ballistic missiles are difficult to intercept because they dive at over five times the speed of sound, according to experts quoted in the report. [1] This challenge is not hypothetical; Ukraine's air defenses have recently failed to stop Russian attacks. According to a report by The War Zone , due to a major shortage of Patriot interceptors, Ukraine was unable to shoot down any of the Iskander ballistic missiles or Zircon hypersonic cruise missiles launched by Russia in an overnight barrage on Kyiv in early July 2026. [4] Iran Conflict and Ukraine Transfers Drained Stockpiles The Iran war â which reaches six months on Friday, Aug. 28Â â has consumed roughly 1,500 of the nation's 2,330 Patriot interceptors, about 65% of U.S. stock, per CSIS data cited in the MEE report. U.S. transfers to Ukraine over 4.5 years also reduced supplies, but the Iran conflict was the "tipping point," said Ed Arnold of theÂ Royal United Services Institute. [1] Production is limited: about 600 missiles are expected to be made this year, with a goal of 2,000 per year by 2030, according to Mark Cancian of CSIS. [1] The strain on U.S. inventories has been building for years. In May 2024, then-National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan stated that the U.S. had run out of "Patriot" missiles to send to Ukraine, noting that "the U.S. Patriot systems right now are being deployed." [5] The cost of these interceptors adds another layer of concern. A single $4 million Patriot interceptor is used against $20,000 to $30,000 Iranian-Russian Shahed drones, creating an unsustainable economic war of attrition. [6] Pentagon and NATO Dispute Reports; Ukraine Seeks More Chief Department of War spokesman Sean Parnell called claims of shortages "false," saying "We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing." NATO senior military spokesperson Col. Martin O'Donnell said it is "simply not the case" that Patriot numbers in Europe are beyond critical, claiming the alliance can "block punches." [1] Ukraine officials continue to request more Patriots, as only U.S.-made systems can stop Russia's advanced ballistic missiles, according to the report. [1] The gap in European air defenses has been a persistent issue. A September 2025 report noted NATO's $400,000 missiles failed to stop Russia's $11,000 drones, and the alliance admitted it lacks 95% of the air defenses needed to protect the region from low-cost, high-volume drone swarms. [7] Meanwhile, European surveys indicate growing desire for strategic independence, with 70% of people in the European Union and the United Kingdom believing Europe should "go its own way" and break free from American influence. [8] Alternatives and Future Production Outlook France's SAMP/T NG system is a potential alternative but has a shorter range and is not battle-tested, according to the report. [1] NATO announced Europe's first Patriot production facility will open in Germany in September, with deliveries to Germany, Netherlands, Romania and Spain beginning next year. [1] Experts note that Russia's war in Ukraine may limit Moscow's ability to launch a sustained air attack on NATO, as it fights on two fronts. The report quotes Arnold: "The uncomfortable truth is possibly the best air defense that we have is Russian constraints." [1] The broader context of Western military capacity is one of strain. As one analysis of American strategic planning put it, "American weapons surely can kill but American military technology, especially its 21st-century creations, far from being 'best in the world' or 'superior.'" Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images UK news Leader of Reform UK in Wales stands down after arrest on suspicion of assault Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, was elected to Senedd as leader of the opposition in May Ben Quinn and Bethan McKernan Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.45 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The leader of Reform UK in Wales is standing down after he was arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault. Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, was announced as Reform UK’s Welsh leader by Nigel Farage in February. He was elected to the Senedd as leader of the opposition in May’s election. However, it emerged on Tuesday that Thomas would not be taking part in questions for the first minister of Wales at the Welsh parliament on Tuesday. Reform said he was absent for “personal reasons”. In a statement on Tuesday afternoon Thomas said: “Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge. I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account.” Thomas is the former leader of Barnet council in north London, but is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly. In a statement, Gwent police said: “On Sunday 13 September a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault … He has been bailed pending further inquiries.” More details soon … Explore more on these topics UK news Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck87.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Between 150 and 200 people were in the church at the time of the shooting, according to one witness By Jamie Whitehead Â and Â Jacob Phillips Published 23 October 2026, 13:55 BST Updated 1 hour ago Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said. At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday. The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack. In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists". Jordan's King Abdullah II, said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties". Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven. CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church. Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns. Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Security officials and members of the public gathered outside the Greek Orthodox church on Friday Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows. Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee. Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active". "People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said. "Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church." He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went". Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started. "I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic." A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer. "The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening. "People started screaming. The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards". Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan". Figure caption, Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed. Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot. Security measures were also tightened ahead of the visit by King Abdullah II to check on the injured. The atmosphere around the hospital remained tense as the sound of crying and shouting was heard as families mourned their loved ones. Many people appear shocked, frightened and angry. Some expressed frustration at what they described as "a failure to take a tougher approach towards terrorists". Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan. Such violence is rare in the country, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the past. Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media. Additional reporting by Majdi Gousous, BBC Arabic.
